title: Complex Numbers and Phases
summary: Complex arithmetic, modulus, polar form and the difference between global and relative phase.
objectives: Multiply complex numbers and find the distance and angle of the result
Write a number as a length and an angle, and see why a number of length 1 never changes a modulus
Tell a global phase, which cannot be measured, from a relative phase, which can
mission: Phases are the reason the amplitudes of a qubit are complex, so start with the numbers in the editor. Define product (z times w), modulus and phi (the distance of z from the origin and its angle), z_polar (z rebuilt from modulus and phi, so it must equal z), unit and unit_modulus (the number e^{iθ} and its modulus), and rel_phase, the relative phase of the amplitudes a and b (the phase of b minus the phase of a).

prediction.question: Two qubit states, (|0⟩ + |1⟩)/√2 and (|0⟩ + i|1⟩)/√2, are each prepared many times and measured in the computational basis. What do the two sets of results look like?
options: Different: the second state has a complex amplitude, so its odds change
The same, about half 0 and half 1, although the states are different
The same, because the two states differ only by a global phase
prediction.explanation: Both amplitudes have modulus 1/√2 in both states, so each outcome has probability 1/2 either way. The states are still different: the relative phase is 0 in the first and π/2 in the second, and a global phase would have to multiply both amplitudes. Only a measurement that is sensitive to the relative phase, such as one after a Hadamard gate, can tell them apart.

hints: Which of the quantities you are asked for are plain lengths, which are angles, and which are complex numbers? Python writes the imaginary unit as 1j.

NumPy has one function for the modulus and one for the angle of a complex number, and e^{ix} is np.exp(1j * x) with the 1j inside. z_polar is the same number as z written from its length and angle, so a wrong z_polar usually means a wrong angle or a missing 1j.
The relative phase is a difference of two angles, one for each amplitude. Work out the order from the task: b relative to a. The value of unit_modulus should not depend on theta at all.

messages.ok: All values are correct: z has modulus {modulus} and phase {phi}, e^(iθ) has modulus {unit_modulus}, and the amplitudes a and b differ in phase by {rel_phase}.
messages.not_number: The variable {name} must be a single number, but it holds {actual}.
messages.product_wrong: product is {actual}, but z times w is {expected}. If only the real part is off, check the term where i times i appears, which is -1. A result like z + w would mean the numbers were added.
messages.modulus_wrong: modulus is {actual}, but the distance of 3 + 4i from the origin is {expected}. It is a real number, the square root of the sum of the squares of the real and imaginary parts.
messages.phi_wrong: phi is {actual}, but the angle of z from the real axis is {expected} rad. Check that it is an angle in radians, and that it is not the modulus or an angle measured from the imaginary axis.
messages.z_polar_wrong: z_polar is {actual}, and rebuilding z from its modulus and angle should give {expected}. The angle belongs inside an exponential, multiplied by the imaginary unit.
messages.unit_wrong: unit is {actual}, but e^(iθ) is {expected}. Without the imaginary unit in the exponent you get an ordinary growing exponential, not a point on the unit circle.
messages.unit_modulus_wrong: unit_modulus is {actual}, but every point of the unit circle is at distance {expected} from the origin. Measure the length of unit.
messages.rel_phase_single: rel_phase is {actual}, which is the phase of b on its own. A relative phase compares the two amplitudes, so a's phase has to come off.
messages.rel_phase_wrong: rel_phase is {actual}, but the phases of a and b differ by {expected}. Check the order: it is b relative to a, and each amplitude contributes only its angle.
